# Patches applied to the vendored Brython

`brython_runtime.js` and `brython_compiler.js` are cut from one bundle, built
from Brython's master of 11 September 2026 plus one hundred and sixty proposed commits
(`metaclass-getattribute-args`, `iterator-setstate` and `getitem-binding` in two, as amended for their PRs) and five merged
upstream since (#3022, #2996, #2989, #2982, #3125), with **four** edits
made in the file itself afterwards. The wrapper, the integer format and the
`__call__` binding carry a `/* BRYNTIME patch, see BRYTHON_FIX.md */` comment,
the only way to find them again in 1.4 MB; the other edit *is* a comment, so
`@vite-ignore` finds itself.

**The integer format and the `__call__` binding are edited in the built file
only**, not in `vendor-base`, so a re-vendoring drops them: re-apply them by
hand after it.

The commits are Brython's own, proposed upstream and carried here while they
wait, which is what this project has always done rather than hold a fix back.
The one merged upstream is master's `18571ba0d` (#3022), a memoryview's item
decoded by its format and read from the end, which the slice commit below is
written against:

| branch | what it changes |
|---|---|
| `none-is-undefined` | `None` and JavaScript's `undefined` become one value seen from two sides, in both directions. `javascript.UNDEFINED` becomes `None`, `null` and `javascript.NULL` are untouched, and `js_array.tp_repr` converts its elements the way the iterator already did |
| `undefined-str-slot` | `UndefinedType` gains the `tp_str` it lacked, so `str()` of a raw JavaScript `undefined` answers instead of raising about a descriptor with no argument |
| `json-big-integers` | `javascript.JSON` reads and writes an integer past 2^53 with its exact digits, the way the `json` module already did. `stringify` no longer raises on a big integer and `parse` no longer hands back an `int` whose last digits are wrong. Both steps compose with an author's replacer or reviver, and both are skipped where the engine lacks `JSON.rawJSON` or the reviver's source text. `from_json` is this `parse` |
| `jsobj2pyobj-exponential` | a whole Javascript number above 2^53 crosses to Python as the int it is. It was built from the number's shortest decimal, which is another integer above 2^53 and exponential notation from 1e21 up, where `BigInt()` refused it outright. `to_py` reaches this on any large number coming back from JavaScript |
| `mark-compiler-chain` | two comments around the parsing chain in the generated `brython.js`, which is what the vendoring cuts on to build `brython_runtime.js` |
| `fstring-format-spec-quote` | a quote used as the **fill character** of a format specification is escaped before being pasted into the generated literal. `f"{3:'>5}"` emitted `$B.String(''>5')`, and the generated JavaScript stopped parsing — *missing ) after argument list* — on an expression CPython prints as `''''3`. A string constant reaches the emitter escaped when it came from a source literal and raw when it came from a specification, so the escape is applied only to a quote that has an even number of backslashes before it |
| `ob-type-name` | a dict key, a module global, an attribute or a local spelled `ob_type` is the author's. A dict keeps its class under a symbol and its string keys as properties, so the key shadowed the field `get_class` reads first: `globals()` raised a JavaScript error once a module bound `ob_type`, and `d["ob_type"] = "business"` left the dictionary answering a string for its own class. `get_class` takes the symbol first when the object holds it itself, so a dict's `ob_type` is data whatever it holds, a class included. A method's frame held its class under the same field for `super()` without arguments, which now reads it from `__class__`, written beside it already, so `locals()`, `vars()` and `dir()` in a method list the method's names and `locals()` has no name to leave out. It replaces the second commit `dict-proto-key` had, which sent the key to the hash table: dicts worked, and an attribute of that name, read through the own-property path, was lost |
| `get-class-ob-type-class` | a JavaScript object's `ob_type` is its data unless it holds a class: `get_class` took any value there for the class, so `{ob_type: "business"}` failed every attribute read inside the engine. It takes the field only when it holds something with a `tp_name`, the test `call_attr` makes of a class. Written for the merged state of `ob-type-name`, whose `klass` it reads. A getter of that name is still run: reading the field off its descriptor costs 3 to 8 % on crossings and class reads, measured, and is left to a mark by symbol, as a dict has, to propose upstream |
| `js-iterable-converts-items` | the items of a JavaScript iterable, a `Set` among them, reach Python converted as an array's do: `IterableJSObj.tp_iternext` yielded them raw, so a float in a `Set` was a `JSObject` and `f"{x:.2f}"` refused it |
| `null-undefined-hash` | `hash()` of `javascript.NULL` and `UNDEFINED` answers the hash `None` has, the two being equal: it read `__hashvalue__` on them, a JavaScript error, so a `null` from a JSON could not go into a set or be a key |
| `getitem-null-item` | `NULL` or `UNDEFINED` as a subscript is refused as any other object is, `list indices must be integers or slices, not NullType`, where `$getitem1` read `valueOf` on it, a JavaScript error |
| `jsobj-function-tostring` | a function read off a JavaScript object is told from a class by `Function.prototype.toString`, not by its own `toString`, which a JavaScript library may override: a snippet of Svelte's in development mode throws from it, so a Python snippet kept in a JavaScript object and rendered by `holder.fn(…)` raised `snippet_without_render_tag` before it was called |
| `list-eq-left-to-right` | lists and tuples compare their items from the first, up to the first that differs: `list_eq` walked them from the last, so `(1, a) == (2, b)` asked `a == b` before telling `1` from `2`, and an `{#each}` sorting `d.items()` read inside every row it compared |
| `sort-less-than-only` | sorting compares with `<` alone: the comparator asked `a == b` whenever `a < b` was false, so a sort ran an `__eq__` CPython never runs, and one that raises refused the sort. It asks `b < a` instead, which keeps equal items in their order |
| `recursion-error-unlogged` | a stack overflow taken for a `RecursionError` is no more written on the console: `$B.is_recursion_error` logged every JavaScript error it was asked about, `js exc RangeError…` with its stack, a line of debugging left in |
| `repr-deep-nesting` (#3125, merged) | `repr()` of nested containers is limited by the stack, not by the recursion limit: it raised `RecursionError` past a thousand levels, where CPython 3.14 writes as deep as its stack goes. A stack overflow out of the outermost `repr()` is the `RecursionError`, and leaves no object marked as being represented |
| `dict-proto-key` | a dict entry whose key is `"__proto__"` is kept. The fast path for a string key is `d[key] = value`, which reaches the accessor on `Object.prototype`: the entry was lost and the value became the dictionary's own prototype, so `"__proto__" in d` was false and reading it raised `KeyError` on a key that had been written. It goes to the hash table instead, exactly as a string parsed as a negative integer already did, and the four sites that ask whether a key can be an ordinary property now ask it in one place |
| `import-name-invalid-identifier-chars` | the identifier a module's wrapper is read back through is built by one rule, `$B.scope_name`, instead of one per site. The generator replaced every character an identifier cannot hold, the importer replaced the dot alone, so the two disagreed on anything else and `new Function` answered *Arg string terminates parameters early*. Five callers, one definition |
| `escape-module-literals` | the module name and the filename are written into the generated module with `JSON.stringify` rather than pasted between quotes. `src/O'Brien.py` is a legal filename, and it closed four literals in a row — the namespace, the frame, `__file__` and `__name__` — so a valid Python file compiled to JavaScript that would not parse |
| `module-name-quote-literals` | the same for the literals of every def, lambda, class, comprehension, `__annotate__` and type parameter: the frame, `$function_infos`, a class's `__module__`, the filename a comprehension's frame carries. A component under `src/Jean's app/` stopped parsing as soon as it held a `def` |
| `noargs-method-arity` | a builtin method that takes no arguments refuses any, `list.clear() takes no arguments (1 given)` and `takes no keyword arguments`, in the name of the type that defines it. Each type lists its methods in `noargs_methods`, beside `tp_methods`, as CPython flags them `METH_NOARGS`, and `finalize_type` puts the check in the function the descriptor calls, once. Sixty-two said `clear() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given`, counting the instance; forty-four took the argument in silence, `(5).bit_length(1)` among them; `str.casefold` spoke as `set.remove`. The checks the bodies made are gone, so `dict.keys()` and `list.copy()` run twice as fast. It reads the keywords under `$B.KW`, so it depends on `kw-bundle-symbol` |
| `list-sort-keyword-only` | `list.sort` takes keyword arguments only: a positional one raises `sort() takes no positional arguments`, where the message counted the instance, `sort() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given`. `list.sort.__text_signature__` is `($self, /, *, key=None, reverse=False)`, and a bound method carries its descriptor's; the getters answered `undefined`, and now answer `None` where no signature is known |
| `generator-called-from-javascript` | a generator function marks the frame of its caller as holding a generator only when there is one. Called by JavaScript while no Python frame ran, a generator or an async generator function raised `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'frame')` before its first line: a list or set subclass whose `__iter__` yields, walked by JavaScript, among them |
| `iter-non-iterator-message` | an `__iter__` that returns something with no `__next__` raises `iter() returned non-iterator of type 'list'`, where it said `non-iterable` of a list, which is iterable |
| `unhashable-type-name` | `hash()` of an unhashable value names its type, `unhashable type: 'list'`, where it wrote the value, `unhashable type: '[1]'` |
| `unhashable-element-context` | a set element or a dict key refused by `hash()` says what it was refused as, `cannot use 'list' as a set element (unhashable type: 'list')`, at every site that hashes one, through `$B.hash_for`, with the class named by its module and qualified name (`$B.class_full_name`). Only a set lookup said it, and it dressed up a `ValueError` of an author's `__hash__` too; `[1] in {"a": 2}` raised `descr.wrapped is not a function`. Vendored as one commit; proposed upstream as two, `unhashable-element-context` for a set (#3149) and `unhashable-dict-key-context` for a dict (#3150). The qualified name is in neither: it is proposed once both and #3123, master's `__qualname__` of a nested class, are merged |
| `set-update-iterates` | the set operations read the storage of an exact list, tuple or dict only, and iterate anything else. They read any array's storage, so a JavaScript array's floats went in unconverted, as `JSObject`s, and `0.5 in set(values)` was False; a list or dict subclass's `__iter__` was not asked, nor its refusal heard; `issubset` of a dict walked the set as a dict and raised a `JavascriptError`, and now builds a set of a non-set argument, as `issuperset` did. Vendored as one commit; proposed upstream as three, `set-update-iterates` (#3151), `set-dict-subclass-iterates` (#3153) and `issubset-builds-a-set` (#3152) |
| `js-array-list-methods` | a JavaScript array has the list methods that read or change it in place, `count`, `index`, `insert`, `remove`, `copy` and `clear`, where it had only `append` and `extend` and the rest raised `AttributeError`. Done by list's own, with the item converted as `in` converts it; a copy is a JavaScript array |
| `plain-jsobject-mapping` | a plain JavaScript object, of `Object.prototype` or of none, is a mapping of its own keys: `len()` counts them, and `get`, `keys`, `items` and `values` read them where the object has no member of that name, so a `Map`, a `Headers` or any other object keeps its own. `len()` of another object raises as it did |
| `no-arguments-message` | a builtin that takes no arguments refuses one with `globals() takes no arguments (1 given)`, in the plural, where it wrote `takes no argument` |
| `locals-no-keyword-arguments` | `locals(x=1)` raises `locals() takes no keyword arguments`, as `globals(x=1)` does, where it counted the keyword as an argument |
| `nb-args-messages` | `$B.check_nb_args` and `$B.check_nb_args_no_kw` word a wrong count in one place: `abs() takes exactly one argument (0 given)` for a builtin that takes one, `divmod expected 2 arguments, got 1` for one that takes several, where both said `takes exactly 2 arguments (1 given)`. A method passes `true` after `arguments`, and its instance is not counted: `set().add()` said `takes exactly 2 arguments (1 given)`, and says `set.add() takes exactly one argument (0 given)`; `[].append` is named `list.append`. On `no-arguments-message`. The `math` functions call the same checker in the branch `math-argument-messages`, not vendored: `math` is not in the bundle |
| `memoryview-index-error` | a memoryview item write checks, in CPython's order, a read-only view (`TypeError`), an index out of the view (`IndexError`, where it said "read-only memory") and a value its format cannot hold (`ValueError` and `TypeError` in CPython's words, where `-1` was written into the bytearray as is, `bytearray(b'\x-1bc')`) |
| `memoryview-released` | a released view refuses every operation and attribute with `ValueError: operation forbidden on released memoryview object`, where it read and wrote on; `release()` and `__exit__` return None, `repr` says released, and a released view is equal to itself alone. One wrapper at the end of the module, around what each operation does |
| `memoryview-slice-shares` | a slice of a view is a view of the same buffer, an offset, a stride and a length in it, where it was a view of a copy: `memoryview(source)[1:]` read old bytes after `source` changed and wrote into nothing. Reading, writing, iterating, `tobytes`, `bytes()`, `cast` of a contiguous slice and `toreadonly` read through it. Written for the merged state of `memoryview-index-error`, whose item write it extends |
| `call-builtin-unbound` | a builtin held as a class's `__call__`, `len`, `dict.fromkeys` or one bound to its own receiver like `rows.clear`, is called as it is: a builtin has no `__get__`, and only what has one is handed the instance. `$B.$call` handed it to every JavaScript function, so `class Clearer: __call__ = rows.clear` raised `list.clear() takes no arguments (1 given)` when called with none |
| `identifier-nfkc` | an identifier holding a character past ASCII is normalized to NFKC, in `name_from_token`, through a `new_identifier` that now works: `box.ﬁeld` reads `field`, `Ⅷ` is `VIII`, and an accent written in two code points names what the one written in one names, where each raised `AttributeError` or `NameError`. A string is not normalized: `getattr(box, "ﬁeld")` still misses |
| `metaclass-getattribute-args` | a metaclass's `__getattribute__` is called with the class and the name, and an `AttributeError` it raises falls back to the metaclass's `__getattr__` or to the default of `getattr()`, as the instance side does. `type_getattribute` handed it a third argument, so every read of a class it governs raised `TypeError: __getattribute__() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`, `K.__name__` included |
| `item-dunder-mro-lookup` | a subscript assignment `obj[k] = v`, a deletion `del obj[k]` and a slice `obj[a:b]` find `__setitem__`, `__delitem__` and `__getitem__` along the class's MRO, as `obj[k]` already did, and never through the metaclass's `__getattribute__`: a metaclass that hid them refused the operation, and `object()[0:1]` raised `AttributeError` where it raises `TypeError: 'object' object is not subscriptable` |
| `method-descriptor-receiver` | a method descriptor called through its type checks that its receiver is an instance of the type, as the getset descriptor beside it already does: `list.append(K(), 5)` and `dict.get(K(), 1)` answered `None` where they raise `TypeError: descriptor 'append' for 'list' objects doesn't apply to a 'K' object`, and `str.upper(1)` raised a `JavascriptError` |
| `int-conjugate` | `int.conjugate()` returns the int, `True.conjugate()` included, where its body was empty and it returned nothing (#3053) |
| `float-conjugate` | `float.conjugate()` returns the float, where it raised `NotImplementedError` (#3044) |
| `int-format-large` | `int.__format__` converts with `nb_float` before handing a float specification to `float.__format__`. `fast_float` wraps without converting, so an int of 2^53 or more arrived as a `BigInt` and `format(2 ** 53, '.2f')` raised `JavascriptError: Cannot convert a BigInt value to a number`; an int no double holds now raises CPython's `OverflowError` |
| `remove-iter-debug-log` | the two unguarded `console.log` calls on the path where `iter()` refuses an `__iter__` that returns a non-iterator are removed. They dumped the object and its class to the console before the `TypeError`, once per refusal; the function's three other traces are behind its `test` flag |
| `coroutine-returned-is-not-dropped` | a coroutine is reported as never awaited when it is reclaimed without having started, through a `FinalizationRegistry`, and no longer when the frame that made it is left. One kept, returned to its caller or handed to `{#await}` and awaited later says nothing, as in CPython; one thrown away, or left in a local that dies, is told once the garbage collector takes it. Only the coroutines not started when the turn ends are registered |
| `reproducible-compile-ids` | `$B.id_counter(n)` sets the counter the code generator numbers functions with, private and started at random, and returns its previous value. `compile()` sets it from the file's path, with `$B.lambda_magic`, so one source compiles to one text in every build, and gives both back after |
| `str-subclass-keyword` | A `**` mapping whose key is a subclass of str was matched against the parameter names as an object: `g(**{T("text"): 1})` raised `unexpected keyword argument '[object Object]'`, a builtin and `dict()` raised `keywords must be strings`. The key names the argument by its value now, and stays itself in `**kwargs` and in `dict()` |
| `del-global-any-order` | `del` took a name out of its scope at compile time, so only the code compiled after it read the name through the lookup that raises NameError: a function written above the one doing `global count; del count` still read `count` directly and got `undefined`. The symtable now records every name a `del` targets, and a global among them is always read through the lookup, bound at the top of the module or in one of its `if`, `for` or `with` blocks |
| `identity-before-equality` | `list.index`, `tuple.index` and `list.remove` compared by equality alone, where `in` and `count` test identity first: `x = float("nan"); [x].index(x)` raised `ValueError`, and so did an object whose `__eq__` answers False. They test identity first now |
| `nan-is-identity` | `$B.$is` answered True for any two NaN floats, so a container comparing its members by identity-or-equality found two distinct NaNs equal: `(float("nan"),) == (float("nan"),)` and `float("nan") in [float("nan")]` were True where CPython says False. Only the same NaN object is itself now |
| `kw-bundle-symbol` | a call's keyword arguments travel under a symbol, `$B.KW`, and no longer under a `$kw` key. A JavaScript object passed as an argument and carrying `$kw` was taken for them: `f(obj)` raised `unexpected keyword argument '0'`, `dict(obj)` answered `{'0': 'a'}`, and `tojson(to_js({"$kw": …}))` refused its own argument. No argument can carry a symbol key |
| `pyobj2jsobj-hook` | an extension point: `pyobj2jsobj` asks `$B.pyobj2jsobj_hook` first, and a result other than `undefined` is the conversion. The engine converts the arguments of every JavaScript call it makes with `pyobj2jsobj`, a local nothing outside can replace, so an application embedding Brython had no way to convert a value itself. Bryntime sets it so a Python callable crosses as `pyHandler` publishes it, trimmed to its arity before anything is read, one identity at every crossing, and a Python list, tuple or dict as a named import's arguments cross |
| `callable-instance-to-js` | `pyobj2jsobj` converts an instance of a class defining `__call__` into a JavaScript function, as it does a function and a method. It handed the object over, so `window.call(C())` raised `f is not a function` |
| `bound-method-js-identity` | `pyobj2jsobj` keeps one JavaScript function per bound method, keyed on its instance and function. A bound method is a new object at each read, and the cache was on that object, so `same(h.run, h.run)` was false and `removeEventListener(h.run)` never removed what `addEventListener(h.run)` added |
| `js-method-receiver-cache` | the Python function made for a JavaScript method is kept in a WeakMap keyed on its receiver rather than in a property written on it. A frozen, sealed or non-extensible receiver refused the property, so every read of `box.run` made a new function and a registry could not remove what it had been given |
| `pyobj2jsobj-graph` | the arguments of one JavaScript call are converted with one memo, and a list or dict is registered in it before its items are walked. `same(rows, rows)` handed over two arrays, and `rows.append(rows)` overflowed the stack. The memo is handed to the hook as its second argument, which is how Bryntime's conversion keeps the same graph |
| `callable-type-slot` | `callable()` asks the type's `tp_call`, the slot `$B.$call` uses, instead of `hasattr(obj, "__call__")`. An object whose `__getattr__` answers every name, or one given a `__call__` attribute of its own, was callable, so a configuration object crossed to JavaScript as a function and `tojson` refused it as a call |
| `json-parse-str-subclass` | `javascript.JSON.parse` reads a subclass of str by its value. It was handed to `JSON.parse` as the object Brython keeps it in, so `JSON.parse(Text('{"answer": 42}'))` raised `"[object Object]" is not valid JSON`. `from_json` is this `parse` |
| `bases-set-subclass-mro` | a class given new bases, `C.__bases__ = (B,)`, reorders its subclasses too, where only the class itself was: `D(C)` kept finding the name on `C`'s old base. An assignment a subclass's order refuses leaves every class as it was |
| `bases-set-moves-subclass` | a class given new bases leaves its old bases' `__subclasses__()` for the new ones', where it stayed under the old: a second change higher up then missed it. Written for the merged state of `bases-set-subclass-mro` and `subclasses-held-weakly`, whose `remove` it calls |
| `subclasses-held-weakly` | a class's subclasses are held weakly, so a class nobody refers to any more is collected: every base kept every subclass it ever had, a class a component makes once per mount among them. The registry pushes, removes, and yields the live ones, so its readers are unchanged |
| `bases-set-validates` | new bases CPython refuses are refused before anything changes: an empty tuple, a value that is no class, a cycle, and bases whose instances are laid out otherwise (CPython's `compatible_for_assignment`, read from the GC flag, the builtins' sizes and offsets, and the slots a class declares, kept sorted at its creation as CPython's `ht_slots`). All were taken, `(1,)` raising a JavaScript error half way |
| `slots-valid-identifiers` | a slot is an identifier given as a string, and `__dict__` or `__weakref__` is declared once, whether the class comes from a statement or from `type()`, which took any name and raised a JavaScript error on one that is no string. A marker a base already has is still taken: Brython's own stand-ins for CPython's C types, `_weakref.ref` and `_socket.socket`, are Python classes with a `__dict__` and a `__weakref__`, under which the standard library declares its own. A single name keeps its declaration in the class's dict, where a class statement put an array in its place. Written for the merged state of `bases-set-validates`, whose `$slots` it reads |
| `bases-set-resets-slots` | a class given new bases updates its `__base__` and what it, and its subclasses, resolved along the hierarchy: `__call__`, `__iter__`, `__init__`, `__new__`, `__setattr__`, `__getattr__`, `__get__`, `__set__`; they kept the old base's |
| `compile-ast-optional-none` | what `compile()` hands to `exec()` runs where its tree leaves an optional field out: the field came back from the Python tree as None rather than empty, and a method, a bare `return`, a slice, a `**`, a `with` with no `as` raised a JavaScript error, the Brython console's every class with a method among them (since master's `113f7097c`). A page's runtime has no parser; the compiler's engine runs it |
| `mro-error-message` | bases with no consistent MRO are refused in CPython's words, naming the bases left in the merge, where the message said an inconsistent hierarchy |
| `slots-class-variable-conflict` | a slot named as a class variable is refused (`'x' in __slots__ conflicts with class variable`), where the class was made and its `x` was neither; `__qualname__` and a `__doc__` no docstring set are not class variables here |
| `slots-variable-size-base` | nonempty `__slots__` on a subclass of a base whose instances vary in size, a `tuple`, an `int`, `bytes`, is refused as CPython refuses it, where the class was made |
| `slots-shadowed-storage` | a slot a subclass redeclares has a storage of its own, where both shared `slot_value_<name>`: a write through the base's descriptor changed `obj.x`, and `del obj.x` emptied both. `__getstate__` reads each slot through its descriptor, and the runtime reads them all that way (`slotValues`), never by the storage's name |
| `slots-str-subclass` | a str subclass in `__slots__` is a name, declared alone or as an item, where it was iterated as a sequence of names or refused as no string; an identifier holding an astral character is refused as no identifier rather than as no string. Written for the merged state of `slots-valid-identifiers` |
| `slot-deleted-descriptor` | a slot written once its descriptor is deleted raises `AttributeError`; a leftover of the former slots wrote into a property that no longer exists and raised a JavaScript error |
| `descriptor-set-returns-none` | the `__set__` and `__delete__` of a builtin descriptor, a slot's or a property's, return None, and `__delete__` is named so; they returned undefined, which the console printed. The runtime wraps the two methods Brython built, keeping their answer |
| `for-loop-inum` | a `for` loop hands its position to the iterator rather than writing it on the value it walks: in a module, which runs strict, a loop over a str raised a JavaScript error, and a JavaScript array walked kept a symbol of Brython's |
| `str-subclass-iteration` | a str subclass iterates over the characters it holds, where it called a JavaScript protocol it does not have |
| `str-keeps-its-characters` | `str()` and `repr()` give the characters as they are: a zero-width space was put before a combining character, and astral characters were counted twice afterwards |
| `str-slice-step-astral` | a slice with a step counts characters, where it stepped through UTF-16 code units and cut astral characters in two |
| `write-str-check` | the console's `write()` takes any str, where it refused one holding an astral character and a str subclass: with `str-keeps-its-characters`, `print("😀")` raised |
| `str-subclass-arguments` | a str method reads a str subclass by its value, as receiver or argument: `join` wrote `[object Object]`, `lstrip()`, `startswith`, `endswith` and `rpartition` raised a JavaScript error, `find`, `index`, `split` and `replace` missed, `encode` encoded the object; `normalize_start_end` reads the value once for every method that takes a start and an end |
| `str-astral-positions` | `partition`, `splitlines`, `endswith`, `replace` with an empty pattern, the width and precision of `format()` count characters, where they mixed UTF-16 positions with them. Written for the merged state of `str-subclass-arguments` |
| `str-astral-results` | what a str method returns goes through `$B.String`, as `%` and `+` already did, so an astral character in it counts once: `len("😀a".upper())` was 3, and so for `join`, `strip`, `split`, `replace`, `ljust`, `zfill`, `title`, `*` and `bytes.decode` among others |
| `str-center-margin` | `center()` puts the odd fill char left when the width is odd too, and counts an astral character once |
| `float-str-subclass` | `float()` reads a str subclass by its value when it defines no `__float__`, where it refused it as no string |
| `class-getitem-raw-key` | `__class_getitem__` receives the key as written, `Box[3]` handing `3` and not `(3,)`; a builtin generic puts its arguments in a tuple itself |
| `classmethod-hook-function` | only a plain function given as `__class_getitem__` or `__init_subclass__` is made a classmethod; a staticmethod or a callable was wrapped and raised. The `__init_subclass__` half is `init-subclass-classmethod`'s |
| `class-dict-kept` | a `__dict__` a class defines is kept, where class creation put its own descriptor over it |
| `set-name-every-key` | `__set_name__` is called for every name of a class, `__doc__` and `__module__` included |
| `bytes-iterator-keeps-position` | a bytes iterator asked for its iterator keeps its position, where `list(it)` started it over |
| `bytearray-iterator-live-length` | a bytearray iterator reads the size its bytearray has now, and stays exhausted once it is: after `clear()` it yielded undefined, after `append()` it stopped short |
| `str-translate-errors` | `translate()` keeps a character only on a `LookupError` of its table, where any error did, and takes a str (a subclass or an astral one included), None or a code point, refusing anything else as CPython does, where it dropped it |
| `write-returns-count` | the console's `write()` returns the number of characters written, where it returned None |
| `iterator-length-hint` | `__length_hint__` of a list, tuple, str, bytes, bytearray, range or reversed list iterator is what remains, where it was the whole sequence; list and tuple iterators keep an index, a list's read live and exhausted for good |
| `iterator-setstate` | `__setstate__` of those iterators moves them, the integer brought within bounds as CPython does (`$B.clip_index`), and leaves an exhausted one alone, where list, tuple and reversed list ignored it and the others took any value. Written for the merged state of `iterator-length-hint`, `bytes-iterator-keeps-position` and `bytearray-iterator-live-length` |
| `sequence-iterator-position` | an iterator over a `__getitem__` sequence keeps its position through `iter()` and stays exhausted, where it started over and read the sequence again |
| `getitem-binding` | `__getitem__` is bound like any special method (`$B.call_special`, through the `tp_descr_get` of its type), in subscription, iteration, `reversed()`, `**` and `dict()`, where a staticmethod, classmethod or property raised TypeError and a callable instance a JavascriptError |
| `hasattr-attribute-error` | `hasattr()` answers False for an AttributeError only and lets any other error through, where it answered False for all |
| `dict-subclass-copy` | `copy()` of a dict subclass copies its items, where it returned an empty dict |
| `dict-update-arg` | `dict(arg)` and `dict.update(arg)` share one reading of `arg` (`dict_update_arg`): a dict that keeps the iteration of dict from its storage, another object with `keys()` through `keys()` and subscription, refusing one without `__getitem__`; `update()` refuses a second argument. In vendor-base, the older `dict.tp_init` is routed through it too |
| `round-exact` | `round()` calls the `__round__` of the type; `int.__round__` rounds in integers, `float.__round__` from the exact binary value, a float with `ndigits`, `ndigits` read through `__index__` |
| `isinstance-reported-class` | `isinstance()` reads the `__class__` an object reports when its class redefines it, as a proxy does |
| `isinstance-list-refused` | `isinstance()` refuses a list where it takes a tuple of types (and `Lib/os.py` passes a tuple) |
| `slots-marker-redeclared` | `__slots__` cannot ask for a `__dict__` the base that sets the layout already gives (`gives_dict`: a builtin type with a `__dict__` descriptor, a class without `__slots__`, with `__dict__` in them, or over a base that gives one); `__weakref__` is left alone, Brython having no weak references and emulating builtin types in Python |
| `solid-base-slot-markers` | `__dict__` and `__weakref__` in `__slots__` do not make a class a solid base, so they no longer conflict with a base that has slots |
| `class-frame-left` | a class statement that raises leaves the frame of its body, where the frame stayed on the stack and the caller read its locals in it |
| `list-copy-not-mapped` | the copy `pyobj2jsobj` makes of a list is not mapped back to the list in `PYOBJ_MAP`, so JavaScript and Python share it (Brython's test 2474 no longer stops on an `alert`). Upstream reached that test by reading arrays before the map (354c98df0), which would send a runtime view back as a JavaScript array; this keeps the map first |
| `bytes-search-bounds` | `count`, `find`, `rfind`, `index`, `rindex`, `startswith` and `endswith` of bytes and bytearray adjust their bounds as CPython does (`search_bounds`), where `count` ignored them, `index` dropped the last byte and `startswith` took no end; the error of an `__index__` passes through |
| `enumerate-start` | the start of `enumerate` is an index (`__index__`, bool, big int) counted as a Python int, where it was kept as given and incremented in JavaScript |
| `builtin-iterator-subclass` | a subclass of `enumerate`, `filter`, `map`, `zip` or `reversed` makes instances of the subclass, with a `__dict__`, where `enumerate` and `filter` made base instances |
| `zip-no-argument` | `zip()` with no iterable is empty, where it raised a JavascriptError |
| `str-search-bounds` | `find`, `rfind`, `index`, `count`, `startswith` and `endswith` adjust their bounds as CPython does (`normalize_start_end`), where they searched past the end bound, matched an empty pattern past the string and counted it in UTF-16 units |
| `str-maketrans-astral` | `maketrans()` reads characters, where it read UTF-16 code units and made two entries, or refused, for an astral one |
| `method-qualname-kept` | a method keeps the `__qualname__` the compiler gave it, where class creation rewrote it: a method of a local class lost its `<locals>` path, and a function stored by `type()` took the class's name |
| `mro-duplicate-base` | a base written twice is refused as `duplicate base class A`, where the MRO reported an inconsistent hierarchy |
| `solid-base-builtin-layout` | a builtin laid out apart from its base is its own solid base, as by its size in CPython: `class X(list, dict)` is refused, and `class X(A, list)` lays out on `list` |
| `init-subclass-classmethod` | an `__init_subclass__` written in a class body is a classmethod, as `__class_getitem__` already was: `vars(C)["__init_subclass__"]` was a function, and `C.__init_subclass__` a function not bound to `C` |
| `super-type-no-instance` | a `super()` whose second argument is its own start type hands what it finds no instance: `super(C, C).prop` is the property, where its getter ran with the class as `self`, `super(C, C).method` the function, where it was bound to the class, and `super(C, C).__dict__` the descriptor. On `init-subclass-classmethod`, which the class statement's own `super()` call relied on |
| `slots-no-dict-descriptor` | a class whose `__slots__` leave out `'__dict__'` gets no `__dict__` descriptor, so its instance raises `AttributeError` for `__dict__`, where it answered a JavaScript `undefined` |
| `vars-dict-attribute` | `vars(obj)` reads the `__dict__` attribute, where it read the engine's dictionary: `vars(C)` of a class is its mappingproxy, where it was a dict anyone could write the class through, and a read of a class's names through `vars()` is a read Bryntime follows. On `slots-no-dict-descriptor`, without which `vars()` of a slotted instance answered `undefined` |
| `dict-has-own-property-key` | a dict asks its own properties through `Object.hasOwn`, where `self.hasOwnProperty(key)` called the value of a key `"hasOwnProperty"` and raised a JavascriptError, a class with such an attribute included |
| `attribute-has-own-property` | an attribute lookup asks the instance's dict through `Object.hasOwn`, where `own_dict.hasOwnProperty(attr)` raised for an instance or a function holding an attribute `hasOwnProperty`. On `dict-has-own-property-key`, through which the attribute is written |
| `dict-literal-big-hash` | the hash the compiler writes for a constant key of a dict display is a BigInt when it is one, where it was written as a number rounded past 2 ** 53: `{1.5: 2.5}[1.5]` raised KeyError |
| `dict-str-key-removed` | a str key taken out of a dict that has other keys, by `del`, `pop()` or `popitem()`, leaves the property it was also stored as, where `get()` still found it |
| `dict-lookup-after-popitem` | a lookup that meets the entry `popitem()` left in its bucket removes it by its index, where it spliced an undeclared `i` and raised a JavascriptError, `3 in d` after `d.popitem()` |
| `list-subclass-iter` | `list()` and `tuple()`, and so `sorted()`, `[*r]` and `f(*r)`, copy the storage of an exact list or tuple only, and iterate a subclass, whose `__iter__` may yield other items |
| `min-max-subclass-iter` | `max()` and `min()` read the storage of an exact list or tuple only, and iterate a subclass |
| `dict-pair-subclass-iter` | `dict()` takes a pair as it is only for an exact list or tuple, and iterates anything else: a subclass, and a JavaScript array, whose items it converts, where a float stayed a JavaScript number no float key found. On `min-max-subclass-iter`, whose iterator it reads the pair with |
| `bytes-subclass-iter` | `bytes()` and `bytearray()` take the items of an exact list or tuple as they are, and iterate anything else: a subclass, and a JavaScript array, whose float is now refused, where it made a byte of it. On `list-subclass-iter`, which they read it through |
| `variable-has-own-property` | a namespace is asked for a name through `Object.hasOwn`, where `ns.hasOwnProperty(name)` called the value of a variable `hasOwnProperty`: once a module or a function bound it, a name assigned again, read unbound or deleted unbound raised a JavascriptError, and so did `f_builtins`. A namespace with no prototype answers too, and the proxy `exec()` makes of a mapping of locals is still read through its `__getitem__`, where the missing method was what sent it there. On `dict-has-own-property-key`, through which a module's dict holds the name |
| `argument-has-own-property` | the arguments of a call are asked through `Object.hasOwn`: a function with a parameter `hasOwnProperty`, given a keyword or a default, and a builtin given a keyword `hasOwnProperty`, raised a JavascriptError where CPython binds or refuses it. The function's half is on `dict-has-own-property-key` |
| `pattern-keyword-has-own-property` | a class pattern's keywords are asked through `Object.hasOwn`, where `case P(1, hasOwnProperty=2)` raised a JavascriptError |
| `unpacked-keyword-inherited-name` | a keyword unpacked into a builtin is told given twice by `Object.hasOwn`, where `kwa[key] !== undefined` found `constructor`, `toString` or `valueOf` on `Object.prototype`: `'{x}'.format(**{'constructor': 2}, x=1)` raised `got multiple values` |

It used to be ten. Eight went upstream, one branch each, and the re-vendoring of
2026-09-11 took them back as ordinary Brython:
`filename-invalid-identifier-chars`, `comprehension-leaks-target`,
`fstring-middle-position`, `remove-jsclass-getattro-debug-log`,
`pyobj-backref-weakmap`, `to-dict-array-to-list`, `expose-unindent`,
`find-start-position`.

| Still edited in place | What it buys |
|---|---|
| the whole file wrapped in `if (!(globalThis.__BRYTHON__ && globalThis.__BRYTHON__.ast))` | a second execution in one process rebuilds `$B.ast`, and the classes the compiler holds lose the `to_js()` the code generator attached |
| `/* @vite-ignore */` on the two dynamic imports | Brython loads JS modules named from Python with `import(variable)`, which Vite cannot analyse and warns about twice on every dev-server start |
| the integer format: `preformat` in `int_funcs`, and the `=` branch of `$B.format_width` | CPython's order for an int with a base prefix. The sign comes first, `-0xf` where Brython wrote `0x-f`, and a `0` fill goes after sign and prefix, `0x0f` where Brython wrote `00xf`. Right upstream too, and not yet sent there |
| `$B.$call`: a `__call__` that is not a function goes through its `__get__` first | CPython's `slot_tp_call`, which binds before it calls. `@classmethod def __call__` gets its class, where Brython raised `object is not callable`; a `@staticmethod` one keeps its answer. Proposed upstream as `call-slot-descriptor` (#3128), and kept here as an edit rather than a commit of `vendor-base` |

Wrapping the file works because `var` keeps its module scope inside a block, so
the 1.4 MB below is untouched: two added lines, top and bottom.

**Two `@vite-ignore`, and it was eighteen.** The other sixteen sat on
`$B.$import(...)`, which is Brython's own function and not a dynamic import, so
`vite:import-analysis` never looked at them; `$B.$import(` merely contains
`import(`. Measured by removing them and counting what the dev server says:
eighteen gives none, two gives none, none gives exactly two, at `import(ref)`
and `import(refs[0])`. They cost nothing at run time and sixteen edits to
re-apply at every re-vendoring.

**Both would be wrong upstream.**

The file wrapper answers a *second execution in one process*, a build tool
requiring the same file twice, or a server rendering after the compiler has run.
A browser loads the script once per page, so the guard protects nothing there
while changing the top-level shape of the file for everyone.

`/* @vite-ignore */` is a comment addressed to **one bundler**. It means nothing
to esbuild, to Rollup on its own, or in a browser. A build tool's annotation has
no place in an engine that is not built with it.
